title: SSCXWC26BHAM: The Facilitators Made Me Do It – Summer Hanson, Bobby Arispe, Zach Hale, & Quinn Kelly
content:
Summer Hanson raced the Women’s and Non-Binary (WNB) Single-Speed Cyclocross World Championships in Bellingham. Why? Because the facilitators made her do it…

“It won’t be where you left it,” a stranger tells me as I approach the bikes strewn in the mud at the start line. I lay my bike down, pausing to consider taking off my lights to hand them to someone I vaguely know nearby. “Don’t overthink it!” someone shouts at me. I leave the bike on the ground and run off to the crowd of women and non-binary folks on the other side of the imposing wooden gate.

Commanding facilitator voices direct us, “Walk backward! More! Okay, come back this way a little!” I’m jostling with ladies and theys with tops bursting to reveal pregnant bellies and titties with hamburger pasties. I’m swimming in colorful wigs, human banana slugs, and psychedelic quilted shark people. I am captivated by the most toned legs I’ve ever seen on display beneath stretchy daisy dukes.

Someone in a tutu compliments my outfit, admiring my confidence. I look down at my tiger-print underwear (with a tiger’s face on the butt) and tell them I’d planned to wear shorts, but after finding out we’d be watersliding into the quarry, I decided I’d rather not spend the rest of my day in wet denim. This is just what I had on underneath.

Better Together

A facilitator, Katie Staver, announces that this is the biggest field of women and nonbinary racers in a Single Speed Cyclocross World Championship race in its 20-year history, with around 100 women and 21 non-binary racers. I ponder the collective peer pressure that helped make this happen, and question how we are defining “world championship,” as I look around at the mostly white American (and perhaps some Canadian) people around me.

The Single Speed Cyclocross World Championship in Bellingham was only my second cyclocross race after stoking a tandem at last year’s Woodland Park Grand Prix. Until I removed the shifter and pushed in the derailleur limit screws on the ’90s Bianchi Advantage hybrid bike I borrowed from my workplace two days earlier, I had never ridden a singlespeed bike in my adult life. I’ve always thought singlespeeding seemed stupid and unnecessarily difficult, but I’m learning that’s the point. I’m here because of the storm of excitement in Seattle’s “alternative” cycling culture, not far from the glorious bike utopia of Bellingham, the event’s host city this year.

I’m a mechanic at Bike Works, a social justice-oriented bike nonprofit in South Seattle, whose work includes restoring and redistributing tons of used bikes that are donated by the community. It’s the type of job that people dream of doing when they retire, but it’s actually a job one can have, with some acceptance of being kind of cash poor, but rich in obscure vintage bike parts, tattered bike zines from the ’90s, and bike nerd friends to hang out with all day. I also organize events and lead social rides for Sound Break, a new bike shop and café in Pioneer Square that’s made its way onto the map as a community gathering place for local and traveling cyclists of all stripes.

Single Speed Fervor

My first introduction to the cumbersome acronym SSCXWC26BHAM was during the 7 Deadly Sins of Cyclocross, a cyclocross season kickoff ride/event that I helped promote at Sound Break alongside Becca Book and Rez (Justin Resnick), two facilitators of the World Championship event. The hype continued to drip into my ethosphere from my seasoned superiors at Bike Works. I’d been hearing breathless reviews of the Lookout Arts Quarry, this year’s race venue, from Recycle & Reuse Director Steve Gadingan. He described his otherworldly experience at the Sh’Bang Art Festival as we wrenched on bikes in the warehouse and urged me not to miss the rare chance to attend a bike event there. I’d never heard of SSCXWC before September, but the crazed look in Steve’s eyes convinced me to go watch the final race on Sunday.

A week or so after getting the low-down from Steve, my partner Quinn and I attended our second Lopez Island Time Trial (LITT), a kooky alleycat style campout + race, organized by SSCXWC facilitator Mike Udelhofen & co, in its second year open to the public (and longstanding tradition between friends before that). They offered 100 bonus points to those who registered to either volunteer or race at the SSCXWC26BHAM. As a defending trophy winner at the LITT, I was hungry for any points that were easier to earn than chugging a can of condensed tomato soup, so I signed up to volunteer.

I couldn’t make it to the qualifiers, and I didn’t ride single speed or cyclocross, so I didn’t exactly consider racing. The facilitators, many of whom were at the LITT, didn’t accept these excuses. Before my conversation with facilitator Becca Book ended that Saturday night at Spencer Spit State Park, I was handed a green SSCX26BHAM-branded zip tie for my derailleur and looped into an email thread with Katie, who assured me I could compete in just the Sunday championship race. Yes, Becca was facilitating whilst partying and camping; are you surprised?

I Tried Not To Race

I continued to attempt to weasel my way out of the race by trying to sign up for a volunteer shift, but all of the Sunday slots were closed. Turns out, sponsors adopted sections of the course, lightening the load for facilitators and volunteers. Evil, Transition, PNW Components, Kona, Outbound Lighting, and Cascade Cross all dialed in the course with obstacles, spectacles, smoke machines, jumps, etc. They wore full costumes and came stocked with handups (snacks or beverages that spectators hand to racers) and noisemakers to heckle us. With little race-day help needed, I offered my skills as a photographer and bike mechanic to the facilitators, and they met me with a resounding “RACE!!!” Finally, with a waived registration fee thanks to the Beard Scholarship Fund, and the facilitators’ appreciation for The Radavist, I finally surrendered to the inevitable. This, reader, is how to get over 100 women and nonbinary riders to sign up for a cyclocross race.

For my surrender, I was rewarded with the most fun race I have ever participated in: I slid down a waterslide into the quarry 3 times, biked through bubble and smoke machines, and rammed a 6′-tall beach ball with my front wheel, bouncing it high enough to bike underneath. I’m doused with buckets of water, whipped (with consent) by a dominatrix, and pushed up hills in a genuinely helpful manner. By my third lap, I worked up the courage to take a couple of jumps, screaming, “I’m so scared, I’m so scared!”

Along the way, I had four cherry tomatoes expertly popped into my mouth by strangers’ hands, as well as a pickle, an Oreo, three Nerds Gummy Clusters, several tiny cups and swigs of Rainier beer, bagged wine splashed on my face, a choked gulp of a mystery liquor from Steve’s gigantic flask, and a mouthful of a White Russian that I immediately spit all over the ground (thanks, but I’m vegan!). On multiple occasions, I peered into a cup as I drank the contents, only to see a healthy amount of dirt sprinkled in. That was just part of the experience!

During the race, communication was polite; plenty of “On your left!” At one point, I heard, “Mind if I take this descent first?” before witnessing a red fishnet-clad racer ahead of me skillfully bike down the gnarliest dirt descent on the course. Sheesh, I see you! My cyclocross skills might not have prepared me for the deranged obstacles of this course, but I rode 3 full laps, pushing my bike up hills and keeping my balance while riding 35 mm tires through some of the chonkiest gravel you ever did see. I put my heart into it, and I have the mysterious bruises to prove it.

Badminton

By afternoon, the sun was high in the sky for an unseasonably warm October day. I ran around photographing the men’s race, and swam to a floating dock in the quarry with the Wet Boyz. They’re Steve’s crew of Bellingham homies who brought the party to the waterslide area.

We rounded out the day with an afterparty at Structures Brewing on the waterfront in Bellingham, where delegations from Asheville and Missoula duked it out for next year’s hosting rights with a game of badminton, an obviously important part of singlespeed cyclocross dominance. The stamina of this haggard crowd to party on after three days of chaos sheds light on the depth of some of the long-distance friendships around me.

If the open arms that pulled me in were any indication, cyclists from around the world who like to push their limits without taking themselves too seriously will be warmly welcomed to Missoula next year.
